source_read: PDF, pp. 248-252 (all pages, born-digital text layer extracted with pdftotext -layout; Table 1 and every number used checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi)

claims.overstatement: Milroy's part is worded accurately ('put down to', overlap, medians, editors' calculations labelled). The claim's closing statement that in these studies the people who decided the cause of death knew the measured levels is not stated by Milroy: the paper says only that deaths were grouped by the cause of death that was given, without saying who gave it, on what criteria, or whether the toxicology was known when it was given. Likely, but it should be worded as the editors' inference ('probably', as the MDMA answer words it).
claims.note: Sheffield figures reproduce on the rendered pages (Table 1, p. 250; Results, p. 249). Editors' calculations recomputed: median ratio 3.49/0.483 = 7.23 (about 7, same); with 13 values the median is the 7th value, so the seven lowest values (0.478 to 3.49 mg/L) all lie inside the injury range 0.035 to 4.81 mg/L, so at least 7 of 13 (same). The injury group is the 24 of 28 trauma deaths with MDMA in blood; the other 4 had MDMA in urine only. Specimen: femoral (peripheral) blood at full autopsy; the interval from death to sampling is not given.

anchors.extracted: Blood MDMA at autopsy by group: deaths given as MDMA toxicity, n = 13, range 0.478-53.9 mg/L, mean 8.43, median 3.49; mixed-drug deaths, n = 22, 0.04-41.5, mean 2.90, median 0.76; trauma deaths, n = 24, 0.035-4.81, mean 0.862, median 0.483. Median ratio toxicity/trauma 7.2 (editors' calculation); at least 7 of the 13 toxicity values inside the trauma range (editors' calculation from the median and ranges).

Deaths with ring-substituted phenethylamines on post-mortem toxicology identified from the files of the Department of Forensic Pathology, Medico-Legal Centre, Sheffield, UK; full autopsy with histology; femoral blood, urine and stomach contents analysed (GC-MS, Royal Hallamshire Hospital); 77 deaths, 1992-2008, positive for MDMA, MDEA or MBDB; deaths grouped by the cause of death given (MDMA or related-drug toxicity, polydrug use, trauma). Who gave the causes, on what criteria, and whether toxicology was known at the time are not stated.

28 trauma deaths (homicide 8, vehicle collision 10, fall from height 6, drowning 4); MDMA in blood in 24, 0.035-4.81 mg/L (mean 0.862, median 0.483); MDMA in urine only in the others; other drugs found: ethanol 17, cannabinoids 10, amphetamine 5, cocaine 4, antidepressants 2, ketamine 1.

The author concludes that MDMA, like cocaine and methamphetamine, shows considerable overlap between tolerated concentrations and those seen at death, that the post-mortem concentration cannot give the cause of death without the history and the other autopsy findings, and that there is no specific toxic or fatal concentration, although concentrations were higher in the MDMA-toxicity deaths.

Post-mortem levels may not reflect levels before death: in 5 cases from another study (Elliott, ref. 43) with samples before and after death, ante-mortem 0.55-4.33 mg/L against post-mortem values up to 28.39 mg/L; MDMA undergoes post-mortem redistribution and heart blood tends to be highest.

claims.overstatement: (1) Not supported as worded: 'One death in that series in which samples were taken two days after death ... (Milroy, 2011, second-hand)'. The case is one of Elliott's (ref. 43, a separate study of deaths after hospital admission), cited in Milroy's discussion, not one of the 77 Sheffield deaths; that person also had a serum level of 4.33 mg/L one day before death. Suggested: 'In one death from another series cited by Milroy, in a person who died after admission to hospital, heart blood taken two days after death was about four times femoral blood'. The ratio itself is right (28.39 against 6.19 and 7.25 mg/L: 4.6 and 3.9, about 4). (2) The clause that whoever gave the causes probably knew the levels, exaggerating the difference between groups rather than the overlap, is the editors' inference, not Milroy's; the reasoning is sound, but it sits inside a sentence cited to Milroy and should be labelled as the editors' reading. (3) The claim's quotation about normal recreational use is exact (p. 250, Discussion paragraph 5), and its remark that this was not measured is correct: no living people were sampled.
claims.note: All Sheffield numbers reproduce on the rendered pages: 77 deaths; 17 MDMA, 30 polydrug, 28 trauma, 1 hypothermia, 1 ischaemic heart disease (sum 77); blood values 13 + 22 + 24 = 59, matching the abstract's 59 with MDMA in blood. The paper does not say which 13 of the 17 MDMA deaths are in Table 1; the Results also say that 13 of the 17 were rapid deaths once a water-intoxication death, a myocardial-necrosis death, a delayed hyperpyrexia death and a decomposed body (liver only) are set aside, so the low-level water-intoxication case may not be in Table 1. Text and table differ on the mixed-drug mean (2.78 mg/L in the Results, 2.90 in Table 1 and the abstract); the claim uses neither. Editors' calculations recomputed: 7.23 and at least 7 of 13, same.

anchors.extracted: Sheffield Medico-Legal Centre files, 77 deaths 1992-2008 with MDMA, MDEA or MBDB on post-mortem toxicology; full autopsy; femoral blood, urine and stomach contents analysed by GC-MS; deaths grouped by the cause of death given; certifier and criteria not stated.

MDMA in 73 deaths, MDEA in 4 (2 with MDMA), MBDB in 2. 17 deaths principally attributed to MDMA: 1 water intoxication, 1 myocardial necrosis, 1 delayed death from hyperpyrexia, 1 decomposed body with liver the only specimen; the other 13 known or presumed rapid. Collapse most often at home, then at a nightclub.

30 deaths attributed to polydrug use, 22 with blood MDMA 0.04-41.5 mg/L (mean 2.78 here, against the Table 1 mean on p. 250; median 0.76); 28 trauma deaths (8 homicide, 10 vehicle collision, 6 fall from height, 4 drowning), 24 with blood MDMA 0.035-4.81 mg/L (mean 0.862, median 0.483); plus 1 hypothermia death (MDMA and amphetamine in urine) and 1 ischaemic heart disease death with several drugs at low levels.
59 of the 77 deaths had MDMA in blood: 13 MDMA toxicity, 22 polydrug, 24 trauma (13 + 22 + 24 = 59), so Table 1's 13 are the MDMA-toxicity deaths with a blood value.

MDMA toxicity n = 13: 0.478-53.9 mg/L, mean 8.43, median 3.49; mixed drug n = 22: 0.04-41.5, mean 2.90, median 0.76; trauma n = 24: 0.035-4.81, mean 0.862, median 0.483. Median ratio 3.49/0.483 = 7.2 (editors' calculation); median of 13 = 7th value, so at least 7 values (0.478-3.49) inside 0.035-4.81 (editors' calculation).
In this series the three groups overlapped obviously; mean and median were higher in MDMA-toxicity deaths than in polydrug deaths, and lowest in trauma deaths.

No specific toxic or fatal MDMA concentration; the post-mortem concentration cannot give the cause of death without the history and the other autopsy findings; higher concentrations seen in MDMA toxicity than in polydrug and trauma deaths.

The author takes trauma-death concentrations as likely equivalent to ordinary recreational use and as a baseline for non-fatal concentrations (no living people sampled); concentrations vary with the number of tablets taken and their content, which varies.

Case from Elliott (ref. 43, deaths after hospital admission; not the Sheffield series): heart blood 28.39 mg/L, right femoral 6.19, left femoral 7.25, vitreous 11.93; post-mortem samples taken 2 days after death; serum one day before death 4.33 mg/L. Heart about four times femoral (editors' calculation: 3.9 to 4.6). Also: 5 cases with ante-mortem 0.55-4.33 mg/L and post-mortem values up to 28.39 mg/L; MDMA undergoes post-mortem redistribution.
In deaths from water intoxication MDMA concentrations will be lower because large intakes of hypotonic fluid dilute the blood (citing ref. 17, the author's own earlier review).

Other series cited also overlap: New York (Gill), mean 1.04 mg/L in acute MDMA intoxication deaths against 0.97 in trauma deaths and 0.58 in polydrug deaths; Melbourne, drug overdose 0.03-3.5 mg/L (median 0.05) against trauma 0.03-2.0 (median 1.03); Taiwan, MDMA only 0.48-16.53 against trauma 0.08-3.05 and 0.11-3.05; US survey (Patel), heart 2.02 (SD 2.84) against peripheral 1.12 (SD 1.23) mg/L, difference not significant.

key_findings.correction: Recomputed: median ratio 7.2; with 13 values the median is the 7th, so at least 7 toxicity values lie in the trauma range; with 24 trauma values the median 0.483 is the mean of the 12th and 13th, so the 12 values from the 13th up (0.483 or more) lie inside the toxicity range (0.478-53.9): at least 12, same.

Heart/femoral 3.9-4.6 and femoral/serum 1.4-1.7 recomputed, same. The card correctly places this case in Elliott's study of deaths after hospital admission; the claim cl_mdma_deaths_fatal_level wrongly places it in the Sheffield series (see claims).

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed with a nuance: in the abstract the 13, 22 and 24 follow the statement that 59 deaths had MDMA in blood, so they can be read as the blood subsets; the problem is that the category totals (17, 30, 28) never appear in the abstract.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with high overall and with the domain judgments: small groups, causes assigned by unnamed certifiers on unstated criteria and probably with the levels known, and the trauma group an assumed, not measured, non-fatal baseline. The JBI prevalence checklist is used for a case series as the round directs; METHODS 5.3 lists no instrument for case series, so the editor may want to confirm that rob_vocab accepts this design and instrument pair.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is right: the conclusion (no specific fatal level, overlap) is what Table 1 shows; the main stretch is treating trauma deaths as ordinary recreational levels.
